script: I told them it was out of stock—then I got a surprise offer!. I was at the till, scrolling through the day's sales, when the phone rang. The voice on the other end was that of an older guy—maybe mid‑fifties, probably a regular. He started off with, "I came into your store Saturday afternoon and grabbed a few Record Store Day items." He sounded like he'd already been through the chaos, like someone who'd just survived a stampede. He went on, "When I got to the counter, I asked about another title and the girl said none of your stores ever had it." He didn't say what the title was; he just kept repeating, "And then I got a text from your shop saying I could order it." He paused, like waiting for me to react. "Now that's not very good, is it?" He sounded disappointed, almost like he was ready to throw a fit. I could tell he was about to vent. So I asked, "Tell me again what's wrong." He repeated the same thing, adding that he felt he'd wasted a trip to our store. I could almost hear the old-school "you're welcome" from the back of my mind, but I held off. I checked the system, double‑checked the inventory, and confirmed: the store never received that release. I told him that, calmly. "If the email is inviting you to order it, you can do that on our website." He asked, "What are you going to do about my wasted journey?" I replied, "You did buy three other items you wanted. This one never came in, but you're free to order it online if that email says so." He muttered, "I don't think it's very good service." I was like, "Look, if I was a customer elsewhere and was told something wasn't in stock, then got an email saying I could order it, I'd be happy." I didn't want to sound like a robot, but I wanted to point out that the system was working as intended. He said, "I am not trying to get a freebie. I love your store and just wanted to vent." The call went on for twenty minutes. He spoke slowly, almost like a sermon. I kept my tone steady, didn't let frustration seep in. By the end, he seemed a bit calmer, a bit satisfied that I had listened. I know the day had been a circus—people screaming at a limited Pink Floyd vinyl, the shop looking like a grenade exploded on the pop section, wrappers everywhere. I know I am supposed to listen to complaints, but that call drained me. I am not sure if I fully grasped his grievance, but I let it be. The system was doing its job. I am fine with that.
